---
title: "1. Project Setup"
subtitle: "Do this on Day 1 — every time"
---

The most important rule of reproducible research: **set everything up before you start collecting or analysing data**, not after. Retrofitting version control and archiving at the end of a project is painful and error-prone.

This page walks through everything you need to do on Day 1 of a new research project.

## 1.1 Create your project folder structure

A consistent folder structure makes your project navigable by anyone — including your future self six months from now.

```
my_paper/
├── _quarto.yml            # project config, bibliography, output format
├── index.qmd              # manuscript: intro, methods, results, discussion
├── analysis.qmd           # all R code: cleaning, models, figures, tables
├── data/
│   ├── raw/               # original data — NEVER modify this folder
│   └── derived/           # cleaned data produced by analysis.qmd
├── outputs/
│   ├── figures/           # figures generated by analysis.qmd
│   └── tables/            # tables generated by analysis.qmd
├── references/
│   └── references.bib     # bibliography
└── README.md              # write this on Day 1
```

::: {.callout-important}
### The golden rule of raw data
Never overwrite, edit, or delete anything in `data/raw/`. Your analysis scripts should only ever *read* from this folder and *write* to `data/derived/`. This means you can always re-run your entire analysis from scratch.
:::

### Your `_quarto.yml`

A minimal starting configuration:

```yaml
project:
  type: default

format:
  pdf:
    documentclass: article
    papersize: a4
    fontsize: 12pt
    linestretch: 2
    toc: false
  html:
    toc: true

bibliography: references/references.bib
csl: your-journal.csl
```

## 1.2 Initialise Git in Positron

Positron has Git built in via the Source Control panel — no terminal needed.

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 1
:::
Open your project folder in Positron: **File → Open Folder**
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 2
:::
Click the **Source Control icon** in the left sidebar (it looks like a branch/fork symbol)
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 3
:::
Click **"Initialize Repository"** — Git is now tracking your project
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 4
:::
Stage all your initial files by clicking **+** next to each file (or "Stage All Changes"), write a commit message like `"initial project setup"`, and click the **tick** to commit
:::

### What Git actually does

Git keeps a complete history of every change you make to every file. Think of it as an unlimited undo button with descriptions. Every time you commit, you create a save point you can always return to.

::: {.callout-tip}
### What to put in .gitignore
Create a `.gitignore` file in your project root to tell Git which files to ignore:

```
# R
.Rhistory
.RData
.Rproj.user/
_freeze/

# Large data files (upload these directly to Zenodo instead)
data/raw/*.csv
*.xlsx

# Output files (regenerated by analysis.qmd)
outputs/

# renv cache
renv/library/
```
:::

## 1.3 Push to GitHub

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 1
:::
In the Source Control panel, click **"Publish to GitHub"**
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 2
:::
Choose **Public repository** — this is what allows reviewers and readers to access your code
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 3
:::
Give it a clear name, e.g. `koura-habitat-mesocosm` — use lowercase and hyphens, no spaces
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 4
:::
Click **Publish** — Positron pushes everything automatically
:::

Your code is now publicly available at `https://github.com/yourusername/koura-habitat-mesocosm`

## 1.4 Set up renv

`renv` records the exact version of every R package you use, so anyone can recreate your environment exactly.

In the Positron terminal:

```r
install.packages("renv")
renv::init()
renv::snapshot()
```

This creates a `renv.lock` file. Commit this file to GitHub — it is one of the most important files in your repository.

When someone else downloads your repository and runs `renv::restore()`, they get exactly the same package versions you used.

::: {.callout-note}
### Why this matters
Without renv, a figure that looks one way in your R version 4.3 might look completely different when a reviewer runs it in R 4.1. Package updates change defaults, colour schemes, and even statistical outputs. renv eliminates this problem.
:::

## 1.5 Connect GitHub to Zenodo (one-time setup)

This is the step that makes the GitHub → Zenodo workflow automatic. Do it once and it works for every repository.

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 1
:::
Go to [zenodo.org](https://zenodo.org) and log in with your GitHub account
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 2
:::
Go to your account Settings → GitHub
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 3
:::
Find your repository `koura-habitat-mesocosm` and toggle it **ON**
:::

Zenodo now watches this repository. When you create a "release" on GitHub later (at acceptance), Zenodo automatically archives a permanent snapshot and assigns a DOI.

## 1.6 Write your README

The README is the first thing anyone sees when they visit your GitHub repository. Write it on Day 1 and update it as you go.

```markdown
# Kōura habitat mesocosm study

Analysis and manuscript for: Raven, O.V. et al. (in review). 
[Paper title]. [Journal name].

## How to reproduce the analysis

1. Clone this repository
2. Open the project in Positron
3. Run `renv::restore()` to install all required packages
4. Render `analysis.qmd` to generate all figures and tables
5. Render `index.qmd` to generate the full manuscript

## File structure

- `analysis.qmd` — all data cleaning, modelling, and figures
- `index.qmd` — manuscript text
- `data/raw/` — original unmodified data
- `data/derived/` — cleaned data produced by analysis.qmd
- `outputs/figures/` — all generated figures

## Software

- R version 4.4.x
- Quarto version 1.5.x
- See `renv.lock` for full package list

## License

Code: MIT | Data and content: CC BY 4.0
```

## Day 1 checklist

- [ ] Folder structure created
- [ ] `_quarto.yml` configured
- [ ] README written
- [ ] Git initialised in Positron
- [ ] Repository pushed to GitHub (Public)
- [ ] `renv` initialised and snapshot committed
- [ ] GitHub connected to Zenodo
